name: Doctors
description: This corner building has been serving Forrest Road since 1874, built specifically to house small businesses connected to the old Royal Infirmary, which then stood almost directly opposite. Its two longest-standing tenants both served that hospital trade directly: George Watson, a cabinet and coffin maker, worked from the building from 1884 to 1959, while surgical instrument maker James Gardiner traded there until the early 1960s, eventually closing under pressure from larger manufacturers. After a spell as a barbecue restaurant and then a pub called The Mortar from 1970, the building took on its current name, Doctors, in 1979 - a direct nod to the vanished hospital across the street that had shaped the building's purpose for over a century.
interesting_fact: The pub's name outlived the hospital it referenced by decades - the old Royal Infirmary across the road closed for good when services moved to Little France in 2003, but Doctors, named in its honour, is still trading today.

name: The Kid's Secret Garden
description: Tucked just off Middle Meadow Walk, this small community garden is run as a free, volunteer-maintained space for local children and families, built from reclaimed timber into benches, planters and a hand-painted sign rather than any formal civic design. It sits at the point where Middle Meadow Walk - the tree-lined path laid out from 1722 on the drained bed of the old Burgh Loch - opens out toward the Meadows themselves, making it a genuinely grassroots addition to one of Edinburgh's oldest planned green routes rather than part of its original historic design.
interesting_fact: Spaces like this - informal, community-built gardens tucked into gaps beside major paths - have become increasingly common across Edinburgh's Old and New Towns as local groups reclaim small unused plots of land, and this one is a good example of that wider, very recent trend sitting right alongside 300-year-old infrastructure.
source_notes: No formal published history found for this specific community garden; description based on on-site signage and general context of Middle Meadow Walk (kept distinct from the existing Middle Meadow Walk POI, which covers the path's own 1722 founding history). Google Places lists it as 'The Kids Secret Garden'.

leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: Edinburgh Futures Institute
description: This grand Scots Baronial building, completed in 1879 to designs by David Bryce, was originally the Old Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh - considered, in its day, one of the best-planned hospitals in Britain, with ward pavilions spaced apart for fresh air and reduced cross-infection, set deliberately next to the Meadows for patients recovering. It served as Edinburgh's main hospital until services moved to a new site at Little France in 2003, after which the category-A-listed building sat effectively unused for years before the University of Edinburgh undertook a seven-year, multi-million-pound restoration, reopening it in June 2024 as the Edinburgh Futures Institute - a 20,000 square metre home for interdisciplinary research, teaching and business incubation.
interesting_fact: The building's distinctive clock tower, visible for miles across the city, has stood watch over this stretch of Lauriston Place through more than 140 years and two completely different institutional lives - as one of Britain's most advanced Victorian hospitals, and now as a 21st-century university research hub.
source_notes: History (David Bryce, 1879, Old Royal Infirmary, 2024 EFI reopening) from efi.ed.ac.uk and curiousedinburgh.org. Google Places confirms 1 Lauriston Place. Leg assigned by geography (84m from existing leg-13 POI George Heriot's School Main Building).

name: Simpson Loan
description: Simpson Loan is one of the main streets running through Quartermile, the large residential and office redevelopment of the former Old Royal Infirmary site, mixing sleek modern glass apartment blocks with the restored Victorian hospital buildings around them. Its name honours Sir James Young Simpson, the Edinburgh professor of midwifery who first demonstrated the anaesthetic properties of chloroform in 1847 and introduced it into obstetric and surgical practice right here at the Royal Infirmary that once stood on this ground - making the street name a direct link between the site's medical history and the development built on top of it.
interesting_fact: Quartermile's street names throughout the development consistently reference figures connected to the old hospital's medical history, of which Simpson Loan is one of the most prominent examples - a rare case of new-build street naming in Edinburgh deliberately preserving a site's institutional memory rather than starting from scratch.
source_notes: Naming connection to James Young Simpson inferred from his direct historical link to the Royal Infirmary site (confirmed via Wikipedia/RCPE) combined with Quartermile's consistent medical-history street-naming pattern; no single source explicitly states the naming rationale, so kept as strongly-inferred rather than fully confirmed. name: Lister Square
description: Lister Square is the public heart of Quartermile, framed by the glass-and-steel Quartermile One office block and the surrounding cafes and shops of the development. Like Simpson Loan nearby, its name reaches back into the site's medical history: it honours Joseph Lister, the pioneer of antiseptic surgery whose techniques - developed in the era when this site was Edinburgh's Royal Infirmary - dramatically cut post-operative infection rates and made modern surgery survivable worldwide. The square now functions as Quartermile's main public gathering space, hosting outdoor seating, events and a mix of leisure and retail units built into the restored and new buildings around it.
interesting_fact: Lister's name appears twice within a few hundred metres of this square - once here in Lister Square, and again a few streets away in the separate Lister Housing Co-operative on Lauriston Place, which was itself part-funded through a trust set up in his memory.
